theme: When Israel went out of Egypt, the Jordan fled
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 114 aloud. It is only eight verses long, and it is one of the most compressed poems in the Psalter. It looks back at the exodus and the crossing of the Jordan and sees the whole creation reacting to the presence of God. Read it as a celebration of the two crossings you have been reading about.
settingTheScene: Psalm 114 is one of the Hallel psalms, sung at Passover. It may have been sung in the temple long after the days of Joshua, as Israel remembered how God brought them out of Egypt and into the land. It pairs two events you have just read about: the splitting of the Red Sea and the stopping of the Jordan. The psalm treats them as one great act of deliverance. Its poetry is bold and playful. It does not explain how the miracles happened. It simply asks: what could make the sea flee, the river turn back, and the mountains skip like rams? The answer is the presence of God.
observation: The psalm begins with the exodus: “When Israel went out from Egypt, the house of Jacob from a people of strange language” (v. 1).
Judah became God’s “sanctuary” and Israel his “dominion” (v. 2). The people are his dwelling place.
“The sea looked and fled; Jordan turned back” (v. 3). The two crossings are placed side by side.
The mountains “skipped like rams” and the hills “like lambs” (v. 4).
The psalm asks the sea and river, “What ails you?” (v. 5), as though they were nervous children.
The answer is direct: “Tremble, O earth, at the presence of the Lord” (v. 7).
The God of Jacob turns rock into “a pool of water” and flint into “a spring of water” (v. 8).
The name of God is withheld until verse 7, which heightens the effect.
interpretation:
Psalm 114 is a poem about reaction. The first four verses describe what happened in nature when God moved. The sea saw and ran away. The Jordan flowed backward. The mountains leaped. These are not scientific descriptions. They are the poet’s way of showing that creation itself recognizes its Lord. Water, which can drown an army, is no more than a servant. Mountains, which seem immovable, jump like frightened lambs. If the natural world responds this way to the presence of God, how should we?

Then the poet does something delightful. He turns and interrogates the sea and the river. “What ails you, O sea, that you flee?” It is almost comical. The mighty Red Sea and the flooding Jordan, scolded as though they had panicked for no reason. The answer comes in verse 7: “Tremble, O earth, at the presence of the Lord, at the presence of the God of Jacob.” The poet has delayed the name of God until this point. For six verses we do not know who made the sea flee. When the name arrives, it carries weight: the Lord, the God of Jacob. This is the God who attached himself to a deceiver and made him Israel. The power that shakes the earth is the same power that is committed to a covenant family.

The last verse is the most surprising. After all the shaking and fleeing, the poem closes with a small, tender image: the God who turns rock into a pool of water. This points back to the water from the rock at Meribah, and to God’s care for his thirsty people in the wilderness. The God who makes mountains skip is also the God who provides a drink for his people. His power and his provision are the same.

For Christians, the psalm tells a bigger story. Israel’s exodus and entry are a pattern. Christ passes through the waters of death and brings his people to an inheritance. Paul says in 1 Corinthians 10:4 that the rock in the wilderness was Christ, and in Hebrews, the land is a shadow of the rest to come. Christian baptism is also described as a crossing: we pass through water out of slavery and into a new life.
connection: The psalm draws on Exodus 14-15 (the sea), Joshua 3-4 (the Jordan), and Exodus 17 and Numbers 20 (the water from the rock). It belongs to the Hallel, Psalms 113-118, sung at Passover, and so Jesus and his disciples likely sang it at the Last Supper (Matthew 26:30). Paul interprets the rock as Christ in 1 Corinthians 10:1-4.
application:
Let this psalm reorder your sense of scale. The things that loom large in your life, such as deadlines, diagnoses, or conflicts, are like the Red Sea and the Jordan. They look immovable until God shows up. Name one thing you are facing, and tell it, in prayer, that it is small compared to the presence of the Lord.

Notice also the God of Jacob. If God attached himself to someone like Jacob, he can bind himself to you. His power is not set against your weakness. It is committed to your good.

Finally, take a drink. When you are thirsty spiritually, remember the rock and the pool. Christ is the source. Come to him and drink.
prayerPrompts: Tremble before the God who turns back seas and rivers, in your own words.
Ask him to turn the hard places in your life into springs of water.
Thank him that he is bound to his people by covenant.
